articleHeadline: If so many people live with toxoplasmosis, how dangerous is this brain parasite really? Should I be worried?
articleSummary: One in three people worldwide are infected with Toxoplasma gondii (toxoplasmosis), with the parasite persisting in muscles and brain for life. Most healthy individuals remain asymptomatic. In Australia, congenital infection risk is low (0.17–2.3 per 10,000 births) and routine pregnancy screening is not recommended; infection can cross the placenta, risking fetal blindness and congenital neurological defects. Cats shed toxoplasma only during their first infection, while undercooked meat is a major global infection source. Retinal toxoplasmosis occurs in about 1 in 149 Australians and can cause progressive blindness; reactivation may happen in severely immunosuppressed patients (e.g., after bone marrow transplant or with HIV). France (~50%) and Brazil (~80%) show higher exposure, linked to diet, stray cats, strains, and climate. In humans, correlations exist between toxoplasmosis and certain brain disorders or psychiatric conditions, but these are not proven causes. Laboratory tests detect antibodies, not the parasite itself, so precise parasite location remains unknown.

articleSummary: Mumbai is reporting a surge in leptospirosis cases amid the monsoon floodwaters. Leptospirosis, caused by Leptospira bacteria, spreads when skin or mucous membranes contact water or mud contaminated with urine from infected animals, especially rats; dogs, cattle and pigs can also transmit. Early symptoms mimic influenza or viral fever: fever, headache, muscle pain (notably calves), fatigue, nausea, and vomiting, risking under‑diagnosis. Untreated infections can progress to kidney or liver involvement, lung or brain complications, internal bleeding, meningitis or kidney failure. Diagnosis is strengthened by recent floodwater exposure history and prompt antibiotic treatment. Vulnerable groups include flood‑prone residents, farmers, construction, sewage/drainage workers and rescue personnel; those with wounds or weakened immunity are at higher risk. Prevention emphasizes avoiding floodwater contact, wearing waterproof boots/gloves, covering wounds, good hand hygiene, damp‑clothing changes, sanitation, and rodent control, with medical care sought for fever after exposure.

articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (Bundibugyo variant) persists despite PPE. By 9 July 2026, over 1,700 confirmed cases and about 600 deaths since mid‑May 2026. No medicines or vaccines for Bundibugyo variant; two therapies began testing in early July 2026, with results pending. Until then, patients receive symptomatic and supportive care in isolated facilities. Incubation ~21 days; early flu‑like symptoms hinder contact tracing. WHO targets tracing 90% of cases to map transmission, but logistics and security on the ground complicate response. Disease progresses from a dry phase to a wet phase with gastrointestinal symptoms and possible bleeding. Infectious dose is very small (5–10 virions). Healthcare workers must wear full protective gear—a hood, goggles, FFP2 mask, yellow coverall, gloves, boots—with meticulous doffing and hand disinfection; shifts in gear last about an hour. A patient recovered after treatment.

articleSummary: Dengue fever in India (Gurugram) is marked by high fever, weakness and low platelets, but severe joint and muscle pain—called 'breakbone fever'—can be the most disabling symptom. Dengue may unmask preexisting joint problems and be more challenging for older adults and those with joint replacements; gradual activity and supervised physiotherapy aid recovery.

articleHeadline: What is toxoplasmosis - and how dangerous is the parasite that causes it?
articleSummary: One in three people worldwide have Toxoplasma gondii, causing toxoplasmosis; the parasite can reside in muscles and brain for life, with most healthy individuals asymptomatic. Cats are the definitive hosts, shedding oocysts only during initial infection; undercooked meat is also a major infection route. In pregnancy, maternal infection can cross the placenta, risking fetal blindness, congenital neurological defects, or miscarriage; Australia estimates 0.17–2.3 cases per 10,000 births, and routine prenatal screening is not considered necessary. Dormant infection can reactivate in severe immunosuppression (bone marrow transplant, HIV) causing acute illness, with therapies that may have significant side effects. Retinal toxoplasmosis can lead to progressive blindness, with Australia incidence about 1 in 149. Global exposure is high in France (~50%) and Brazil (up to ~80%). Tests detect antibodies, not the parasite’s location. Rodent studies show toxoplasma can alter brain behavior to enhance transmission to cats, completing its life cycle.

articleSummary: Chandipura virus (CHPV), a rhabdovirus, has caused three pediatric deaths in Gujarat, India, with additional children testing positive. Although rare, CHPV can trigger acute encephalitis within 24–48 hours of infection, especially during the monsoon season when sandfly populations rise. Transmission is vector-borne via sandflies; it is not spread by sneezing or coughing. Children under 15, particularly under 10, are most at risk due to underdeveloped immunity and outdoor exposure. Management is supportive: hospital admission, fever control, seizure management, fluid balance, and ICU care if needed. Prevention focuses on sandfly avoidance: repellents, bed nets, covering clothing, keeping surroundings clean, and eliminating breeding sites.

articleHeadline: Chikungunya outbreak reported in Samar
articleSummary: Chikungunya outbreak in Gandara, Samar, Philippines, with 84 confirmed cases in the villages of Ngoso and Catorse de Agosto. Both villages have been under Code Red since June 30, and the first case was detected in May. The outbreak remains limited to these communities, while authorities monitor 67 other barangays to prevent spread. Chikungunya is transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus—the same vectors that spread dengue and Zika. Symptoms include sudden high fever, skin rashes, headache, fatigue, and severe joint and muscle pains; illness is usually not fatal but can cause prolonged joint pain. Containment actions include cleaning surroundings, unclogging canals, draining stagnant water, and destroying breeding sites. There is no specific antiviral treatment; management focuses on rest, hydration, and fever/pain relief. Seek medical attention promptly; avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen or aspirin without a clinician's guidance, as these can complicate dengue diagnosis.

articleHeadlineTranslated: The 12 de Octubre Hospital develops the first oral vaccine against the most lethal Ebola variant.
articleHeadline: El hospital 12 de Octubre desarrolla la primera vacuna oral contra la variante más letal del ébola
articleSummary: Oral vaccine against the most lethal Ebola variant developed by the 12 de Octubre Hospital. Results were published in two international journals and correspond to the first-stage experimental proof-of-concept, with favorable findings in small animal models. These results show, for the first time with an oral approach, that the vaccine can activate the immune system and protect against lethal exposure. The vaccine uses virus-like particles without genetic material to train the immune system; a single dose prompted immune protein development, while additional doses yielded up to 70% survival after lethal exposure. Oral administration offers logistical advantages over current intramuscular vaccines, reducing need for trained personnel and cold chain, and stimulating mucosal immunity at entry points. The work is a collaboration among Spain's CSIC National Center for Biotechnology, University of Cambridge, and Hamburg's Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine; live-virus exposure testing occurs in Hamburg due to Spain's lack of BSL-4 labs. If successful, human trials could be at least a year away. Parallel mosaic vaccine line targets multiple variants, relevant amid outbreaks like Democratic Republic of Congo with around 400 deaths.

articleSummary: Canine influenza (dog flu) is a contagious respiratory infection primarily caused by viruses, with transmission rising in winter as dogs spend more time in enclosed spaces. Common symptoms include persistent cough, sneezing, nasal discharge, watery eyes, fever, loss of appetite, and reduced activity. In addition to canine flu, winter respiratory diseases such as kennel cough (tracheobronchitis), bronchitis, and pneumonia can occur, potentially requiring veterinary care. For small breeds, seniors, puppies, or poorly furred dogs, consider a warm dog coat. Daily care includes balanced nutrition, fresh water, adherence to vaccination schedules, and routine preventive visits. Avoid self-medication of human drugs, which can mask symptoms and delay diagnosis.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning stated Beijing’s continued readiness to help African nations according to on-the-ground needs and capacities, with ongoing cooperation to accelerate outbreak control. No case counts were cited. The move underscores international collaboration and capacity-building to curb Ebola in the region.

articleSummary: In the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ebola has reached 1,830 confirmed cases and 648 deaths since the outbreak was declared on May 15, according to authorities. The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no vaccine or treatment. This marks the 17th Ebola outbreak in the DRC, with transmission ongoing as of 2026-07-11. Ebola virus disease is known for hemorrhagic fever. The article notes that the deadliest DR Congo outbreak occurred in 2018–2020, with about 2,300 deaths among roughly 3,500 cases. No details are provided on laboratory confirmation or imported/exported cases in the article.

articleHeadline: RDC: inquiétudes après la découverte de quatre cas d'Ebola à Kisangani
articleSummary: Four Ebola cases have been confirmed in Kisangani, Democratic Republic of Congo, with two fatalities and two patients currently isolated and treated. The first two cases involve women who worked in mining areas near Nyanya, Ituri; one was pregnant, and laboratory testing confirmed Ebola. A third Kisangani case is a patient who had escaped after a fire at a treatment center in PK50, Ituri, about ten days earlier. The fourth is a police officer infected in Nia-Nia before arriving in Kisangani. Authorities are conducting exhaustive contact tracing and expanding surveillance in Tshopo to prevent further spread into this large city near Ituri. Entry-point controls and case management are being reinforced to limit risky movements. Ituri still accounts for more than 90% of cases concentrated in five to six health zones, as of 11 July 2026.

articleHeadline: Ebola en RDC : 1 830 cas et 648 décès au 9 juillet, l'Ituri atteint 25 zones de santé touchées
articleSummary: Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has 1,830 confirmed cases and 648 deaths as of July 9, 2026, across Ituri, North Kivu and South Kivu, with a 35.4% fatality. Ituri remains the epicenter, with 25 of 36 health zones affected; Boga in Irumu reports its first confirmed case, linked to a patient from Bunia, raising cross-border transmission concerns. North Kivu has 11 zones affected; Kisangani in Tshopo records two cases (one linked to Nia-Nia) and two cases imported in Wamba, Haut-Uele. South Kivu has three cases and one death in Miti-Murhesa, with over 42 days without a new confirmed case, signaling possible end of transmission there. A health meeting in Bunia addressed payroll delays; WHO cites 1,561 cases and 506 deaths (as of July 7), with Bundibugyo having no licensed vaccine or treatment. A July 2 trial tests MBP134 and remdesivir; neither validated.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Amid a 'serious' stage of foot-and-mouth disease in South Korea, presidents of livestock cooperative associations and others gave massages during a training trip to Vietnam.
articleHeadline: 韓国で口蹄疫「深刻」段階の中、畜協組合長らがベトナム研修でマッサージ
articleSummary: Foot-and-mouth disease triggered a 'serious' alert in North Gyeongsang Province, South Korea, after outbreaks were confirmed at six farms—pig and cattle operations in Yecheon—on the 3rd of the month. The northern six cities and counties, including Andong and Yeongju, were placed in the 'serious' stage. Authorities ordered a 48-hour movement ban on livestock and vehicles and suspended livestock markets to contain spread. Despite restrictions, more than 10 heads of local livestock cooperatives departed on a four- to five-day training trip to Vietnam, leaving July 7 for Nha Trang; itineraries reportedly included a night city tour and a 120-minute full-body massage, later revised to focus on distribution facilities. The association stated the trip was abroad and not domestic gathering, asking media not to broadcast. Gyeongsangbuk-do houses about 745,000 cattle, the largest herd in Korea.

articleHeadline: الصحة العالمية: تفشي "إيبولا" في الكونغو يفوق الأرقام الرسمية بأربعة أضعاف
articleSummary: On 11 July 2026, the World Health Organization warns that the true scale of Ebola virus disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo may be two to four times higher than official counts. WHO Emergency Director Chikwe Ihekweazu says about 80% of new infections have no link to known cases, indicating widespread community transmission, notably in Ituri province. Government data show 1,792 cases and 625 deaths, with around 90% of all cases concentrated in Ituri and the outbreak extending to North Kivu, South Kivu, and Tshopo. Laboratory results from Bunia city reveal high positivity rates, reflecting ongoing transmission despite some containment progress in other areas.
